association: Two variables are associated when knowing one tells you something about the other. In a two-way table, the conditional percents are different from group to group. An association does not prove that one thing causes the other.
bin: One group of values in a histogram. Each bar of a histogram is one bin.
box-plot: A graph that shows the five-number summary. A box goes from Q1 to Q3, with a line at the median. Lines called whiskers go out to the minimum and the maximum.
categorical-data: Data that puts each answer into a group or category, like “bus, car, or walk.” It is not a measurement.
center: A single number that describes a typical value in a data set. The mean and the median are measures of center.
conditional-distribution: The percents for one variable inside a single group. Divide each count in that group’s row (or column) by the group’s total.
data: Facts or numbers that we collect to learn about something.
distribution: All the values in a data set and how often each one happens. A graph of the data shows its distribution.
dot-plot: A graph that puts one dot above a number line for each data value. Dots for the same value stack up.
empirical-rule: In a normal distribution, about 68% of the data is within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% is within 2, and about 99.7% is within 3. Also called the 68-95-99.7 rule.
fence: A cutoff for outliers. The lower fence is $Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$. The upper fence is $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$. A value outside the fences is an outlier.
five-number-summary: Five numbers that describe a data set: the minimum, Q1, the median, Q3, and the maximum.
frequency: How many times a value happens in a data set.
frequency-table: A table that lists each value and its frequency.
histogram: A bar graph for number data. The values are put in groups called bins. The bars touch, and the height of each bar is how many values are in that bin.
interquartile-range: The distance from Q1 to Q3. It shows how spread out the middle half of the data is. Also called the IQR.
iqr: Short for interquartile range: $Q_3 - Q_1$. It shows how spread out the middle half of the data is.
marginal-distribution: The percents for one variable, found from the totals in the margins of a two-way table. Divide each total by the grand total.
maximum: The largest value in a data set.
mean: The sum of all the values divided by how many values there are. Also called the average.
median: The middle value when the data is in order. With an even number of values, the median is halfway between the two middle values.
minimum: The smallest value in a data set.
mode: The value that happens most often in a data set.
mu: The Greek letter $\mu$, read “mew.” It stands for the mean of a population or of a normal distribution.
normal-distribution: A bell-shaped, symmetric distribution. Its mean and median are equal and sit in the center. It is described by its mean and its standard deviation.
outlier: A value that is far away from the rest of the data. A common rule: a value is an outlier if it is more than $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ below Q1 or above Q3.
percentile: The percent of the data that is below a value.
population: The whole group we want to learn about.
quartile: The three values that cut ordered data into four parts with the same number of values. Q1 is the median of the lower half. The median is Q2. Q3 is the median of the upper half.
range: The maximum minus the minimum. It shows how spread out all the data is.
relative-frequency: A count divided by a total, written as a fraction, decimal, or percent.
sample: A part of a group that we collect data from. We use the sample to learn about the whole group (the population).
segmented-bar-chart: A bar chart where each bar is 100% of one group, split into parts. It shows conditional distributions side by side.
shape: What a graph of the data looks like: symmetric, skewed left, or skewed right.
sigma: The small Greek letter $\sigma$. It stands for the standard deviation of a population or of a normal distribution. The capital letter $\Sigma$ means something different: add up.
sigma-notation: $\Sigma$ is the Greek capital letter sigma. In statistics it means add up.
skewed-left: A shape where most values are high and a long tail stretches to the left. The mean is less than the median.
skewed-right: A shape where most values are low and a long tail stretches to the right. The mean is greater than the median.
spread: How far apart the values in a data set are. The range, the IQR, and the standard deviation are measures of spread.
standard-deviation: A number that tells how far the values in a data set usually are from the mean. A small standard deviation means the values are close to the mean. It is often written $s$ (for a sample) or SD.
symmetric: A shape where the left side and the right side look about the same. The mean and the median are about equal.
tail: The long, low side of a graph. The mean is pulled toward the tail.
tally: A mark made for each data value as you count it.
two-way-table: A table that shows counts for two categorical variables at once. One variable goes across the rows and the other down the columns. The totals are in the margins.
variance: The standard deviation squared. To find it, add the squared differences from the mean and divide by $n - 1$.
venn-diagram: A picture that uses overlapping circles to show groups. The overlap shows what is in both groups. The space outside the circles shows what is in neither.
whisker: A line on a box plot that goes from the box out to the smallest or largest value that is not an outlier.
x-bar: The symbol $\bar{x}$, read “x-bar.” It stands for the mean of a sample: $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\Sigma x}{n}$.
z-score: How many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean. A positive z-score is above the mean. A negative z-score is below the mean.
z-table: A table that gives the area under the standard normal curve to the left of a z-score. That area is the proportion of the data below the z-score.
